title: USPTO trademark statistics and 2026 filing trends
summary: US trademark filings hit 664,477 in FY 2026 (+23.3%). Explore 14.4M USPTO records on Class 42 AI marks, $350 filing fees, 4.1-month wait times, and survival.
body_markdown:
US federal trademark filings are climbing again, led by US-nationality owners and software brands. In fiscal year 2026 (October 1, 2025, through September 30, 2026, the October–September window used for annual USPTO totals below unless noted), applicants filed **664,477** trademark applications in our daily Case Files index, up **23.3%** from the 2023 low ( **904,483** application classes in the USPTO’s workload tables, and **664,767** applications in the 12 months ending October 31, 2026). Filings from China-nationality owners remain 35% below their 2021 subsidy peak, while applications from US-nationality owners reached an all-time high of **438,816** in 2026 ( **440,377** in the 12 months through October), passing their 2021 record.


Three years ago, the US trademark register was coming down from its pandemic peak. E-commerce launches and municipal filing subsidies in China lifted 2021 volume to 740,845 applications and pushed first-action wait times past eight months. Filings then fell for two years to 538,806 in 2023, alongside the 2023–2024 contraction in[whether .com is still growing](https://instantdomainsearch.com/learn/guides/is-com-still-growing) and[why domain registrations are growing](https://instantdomainsearch.com/learn/guides/why-are-domain-registrations-growing) . Since 2023, applications have risen three years in a row while the USPTO cut first-action wait times in half to 4.1 months.


Nice Class 42, which covers software as a service, cloud platforms, and artificial intelligence services, grew **65.5%** over three years to 78,190 applications, and one in three Class 42 filings now names artificial intelligence in its goods and services. We examined all **14,425,496** deduplicated applications and registrations in our[USPTO trademark search](https://instantdomainsearch.com/trademark-search) index through November 21, 2026, alongside USPTO workload reports and the January 2025 fee changes, to see where new filings are concentrated and how many reach registration.


## How many trademarks are filed with the USPTO each year?


Before the pandemic, US federal trademark volume grew from 437,206 applications in 2017 to 499,471 in 2019. Volume rose to 560,513 in 2020 and peaked at 740,845 in 2021, including a single-month record of 93,045 applications in December 2020 ahead of the January 2021 fee increase. Filings then fell 22.6% to 573,292 in 2022 and another 6% to 538,806 in 2023.


Volume bottomed in 2023, then rose 7.3% to 578,074 in 2024, 8% to 624,094 in 2025, and 6.5% to **664,477** in 2026, up 125,671 applications (+23.3%) over three years. Between April and June 2026, applicants filed 180,029 marks, the busiest quarter since early 2021.


The USPTO’s[Trademarks Dashboard](https://www.uspto.gov/dashboard/trademarks/) and[annual workload tables](https://www.uspto.gov/about-us/financial-and-performance) report the same turn in **classes filed** rather than distinct serial numbers. Because one application can claim multiple Nice classes (averaging 1.33 to 1.37 classes per application across this window) and Madrid extensions enter on slightly different schedules, we compare the two series side by side rather than mixing them. USPTO classes filed dropped from 943,928 in 2021 to 737,018 in 2023, then climbed to 767,138 in 2024 (+4.1%), 824,192 in 2025 (+7.4%), and **904,483** in 2026 (+9.7%, and +22.7% above 2023).

Grouping applications by the first listed owner’s nationality (` Owner.nationality` in case files, which records legal nationality or state of organization rather than applicant domicile) separates the 2021 spike from the 2026 recovery. Between 2019 and 2021, applications from China-nationality owners more than tripled from 72,021 to 223,932 (30.2% of all US filings), driven by cross-border marketplace sellers and municipal trademark subsidies. In December 2020, China-nationality owners filed 44,623 US applications, briefly passing US-nationality owners (39,734). After those subsidies ended and the USPTO tightened US-counsel rules and sanctioned high-volume filing mills, applications from China-nationality owners fell by more than half to 108,979 in 2023.


In 2026, filings from China-nationality owners slipped 8.6% to 145,880, still 34.9% below their 2021 peak, while all other non-US nationalities held steady at 79,014. Applications from US-nationality owners rose from 351,701 in 2023 to **438,816** in 2026 (66% of all filings), the highest US-nationality total in the USPTO archive.


## USPTO trademark filing fees and wait times in 2026


The growth through 2025 and 2026 arrived despite higher entry-level USPTO trademark filing fees. On January 18, 2025, the USPTO’s[2025 trademark fee changes](https://www.uspto.gov/trademarks/fees-payment-information/summary-2025-trademark-fee-changes) retired TEAS Plus ($250 per class) and TEAS Standard ($350 per class) in favor of a single **$350** base application fee per class in Trademark Center. Applicants who type custom goods-and-services text into the free-form box instead of picking pre-approved entries from the Trademark ID Manual now pay an extra **$200** per class ($550 total), plus **$200** for each 1,000 characters beyond the first 1,000 and **$100** per class for incomplete applications. Section 8 post-registration maintenance fees also rose from $225 to $325 per class, and WIPO Madrid filings rose from $500 to $600 per class on February 18, 2025.


On Friday, January 17, 2025, the final day of the $250 TEAS Plus tier, applicants submitted **7,659** applications in a single day, more than triple a normal January weekday. Volume across January 1–17 hit 47,004 applications before dropping to 14,384 across January 18–31 and 38,443 in February 2025. Like the wholesale fee pull-forwards in` .com` domains, that dip lasted only a few weeks. By March 2025, monthly filings were back at 53,165, and quarterly volume climbed to 165,996 in the first quarter of 2026 and 180,029 in the second quarter.


Examination wait times fell over the same period. After the 2021 backlog pushed average first-action wait times to 8.2 months in late 2023 and total disposal time to 14.6 months, the USPTO’s[2026 trademark review](https://www.uspto.gov/subscription-center/2026/banner-year-trademarks-delivers-faster-service-and-smarter-tools) reported that first-action pendency dropped to **4.1 months** and total disposal pendency fell to **9.5 months** , while unexamined inventory shrank 12% to 305,978 classes. Alongside standardized ID Manual filings and the removal of 14,000 invalid applications and registrations for fraud in 2026, the office launched[Class ACT](https://www.uspto.gov/subscription-center/2026/trademark-classification-goes-agentic-usptos-announcement-class-act) on March 19, 2026, an internal AI system that assigns international trademark classes, design search codes, and pseudo marks in five minutes or less instead of a multi-month pre-examination queue.


## Software and AI in Trademark Class 9 and Class 42


Grouping filings into 12-month windows ending October 31 (matching the window in our` .com` study) shows how Nice classification volume moved from physical goods to software. During the 12 months ending October 31, 2021, **Class 25** (clothing, footwear, and headwear) was the busiest class among all 45 trademark classes in the US system with 92,607 applications, ahead of **Trademark Class 9** (downloadable software, mobile apps, and electronics) at 86,347, while **Trademark Class 42** (software as a service, cloud computing, and technological research) ranked fifth at 50,863.


In the 12 months ending October 31, 2026, Class 25 sat 25.3% below its 2021 peak at 69,181 applications, and other 2021 consumer categories such as Class 21 (housewares, down 34.2%) and Class 28 (toys and games, down 23.8%) remained lower as well. **Class 9** moved into first place at a record **88,704** applications (+31.6% since 2023), **Class 41** (education, training, and online media) rose to 87,542 (+34.6% since 2023), and **Class 42** grew **65.5%** from its 2023 low (47,238 to **78,190** ), including a **39.7% gain in the past year** from 55,979 in 2025. Together, **141,418** applications in the past year claimed Class 9 or Class 42, or **21.3%** of all US trademark filings.


Much of Class 42’s gain comes from AI services. On January 1, 2026, the USPTO[adopted the 13th edition of the Nice Classification](https://www.uspto.gov/subscription-center/2025/uspto-will-incorporate-updates-nice-classification-2026) , adding Class 42 entries for *artificial intelligence as a service (AIaaS)* and *artificial intelligence consultancy* to the pre-approved ID Manual so applicants avoid the $200 free-form surcharge. Across all classes, applications containing the phrase` artificial intelligence` in their goods and services grew nearly sixfold over four years, from 5,649 in 2022 (1% of all filings) to 19,186 in 2025 (3.1%) and **32,517** in 2026 ( **4.9%** , or roughly one in 20 US trademark filings). Inside Class 42, **33.1%** of applications ( **25,868** of 78,190) now name artificial intelligence, up from 7.1% in 2021. In Class 9, that share rose from 3.6% to **16.1%** (14,238 applications).


## AI agent trademarks, ChatGPT, and descriptive terms


Trademark wordmarks followed the same curve we saw in 133.1 million new` .com` domains, on a register where each filing costs hundreds of dollars. After ChatGPT launched in late 2022, USPTO wordmark applications containing` gpt` jumped from nine in 2022 to **319** in the 12 months ending October 31, 2023, peaking at 151 in the second quarter of 2023 (the same quarter first-time` gpt`` .com` domains peaked at 41,200).


Of the 319` gpt` applications filed in the 12 months through October 2023, **216 (67.7%) are dead** , **59 (18.5%) remain pending** (including OpenAI’s own December 2022 applications for` GPT` and` CHATGPT` , with 36 suspended under status code` 654` and 12 in opposition under` 774` ), and **44 (13.8%)** are live registrations. Within the 216 dead records, 138 abandoned after no timely office-action response (` 602` ), 39 ended after an inter-partes decision (` 604` ), 33 were expressly abandoned (` 601` and` 605` ), and one lapsed with no Statement of Use (` 606` ). Bulk case files record current lifecycle status codes rather than the specific refusal grounds inside each office action. By 2026, new` gpt` trademark filings had fallen 71% to 93.


Over 2025 and 2026, founders moved away from model acronyms and toward AI agent trademarks and distinct brand names. Wordmark applications containing` agent` quadrupled from 202 in 2023 to **843** in the 12 months ending October 31, 2026, nine times` gpt` ’s total, while applications describing` AI agent` ,` software agent` , or` autonomous agent` tools in their goods and services jumped from 57 in calendar year 2023 to **1,697** across the first three quarters of 2026 (where literal` AI AGENT` wordmarks face descriptive scrutiny under USPTO examination rules unless paired with a distinctive brand). Most AI software applicants skipped buzzwords in the brand name. Even in 2026, marks containing` gpt` ,` agent` , or a standalone` ai` token account for about 5,000 filings, meaning roughly six out of seven applicants describing artificial intelligence in their goods and services chose an ordinary or coined brand name.

## Live, dead, and intent-to-use trademark approval rates


Across all **14,425,496** case files in our index on November 21, 2026, **3,766,934 (26.1%)** are live registrations, **1,329,638 (9.2%)** are pending applications, and **9,328,924 (64.7%)** are dead or abandoned marks.


Much of that attrition comes from people reserving names before a product ships, the legal equivalent of parking an unused` .com` . In 2026, **47.5%** of applicants ( **315,332** filings) submitted an intent-to-use trademark application under Section 1(b), up from 43.5% in 2025. Across settled cohorts filed between 2017 and 2022, applications backed by commercial use at filing reached registration **73.7% to 77%** of the time, whereas intent-to-use applications registered **37.8% to 45.5%** of the time. Roughly three in 10 intent-to-use filings become abandoned trademarks under status code` 606` after clearing examination because the applicant never submits a Statement of Use. Even after registration, **3.49 million** marks across the archive were later cancelled under Section 8 when owners did not prove continued use between years five and six.


## Trademark vs. domain name availability


In the 12 months ending October 31, 2026, registrants added 32.34 million first-time` .com` names against 664,767 US trademark applications, or **49 brand-new` .com` domains for every trademark filing** . Short names on the federal register are still heavily spoken for. Across **3,339,183** distinct live or pending alphanumeric wordmarks, **92.6%** of all 17,576 three-letter` A–Z` combinations (16,279) are claimed somewhere on the register, including **52.2%** (9,178) in Class 9 or Class 42.


Unlike DNS, where or resolves to one registrant worldwide, trademark law scopes rights to related goods and services. Across our live index, **200,393** distinct wordmarks are held under two or more distinct owner names at the same time, and 23,351 appear under five or more, led by single words such as` TITAN` (197 distinct live owner names),` APEX` (172),` ATLAS` (167), and` ECLIPSE` (155). A taken` .com` does not mean a word is blocked in your Nice class, and registering one of the[popular domain extensions in 2026](https://instantdomainsearch.com/learn/guides/popular-domain-extensions-2026) such as` .ai` ,` .app` , or a prefixed` .com` gives you no defense against domain name trademark infringement if another software company already holds a confusingly similar mark in Class 9 or Class 42.


Public USPTO case files also have clear limits. They cover federal applications and registrations only, so they do not record unregistered common-law rights earned through local or commercial use, state trademark registers, or foreign registers outside Madrid designations. Our wordmark counts also exclude visual conflicts among the 1,509,720 design-only logo records that carry no mark text, and case files cannot tell whether a pending intent-to-use AI filing will ship a real product next year.

## Frequently asked questions


### How many trademarks are there in the US in 2026?


On November 21, 2026, our daily index of the USPTO Trademark Case Files dataset held 14,425,496 total records, including 3,766,934 live registered trademarks, 1,329,638 pending applications, and 9,328,924 dead or abandoned records. Annual filings rose three years in a row from 538,806 applications in 2023 to 664,477 in 2026 (+23.3%), led by an all-time record 438,816 applications from US-nationality owners.


### How much does a trademark cost at the USPTO in 2026?


Since January 18, 2025, the base USPTO trademark filing fee in Trademark Center is $350 per international class when you select pre-approved goods and services from the Trademark ID Manual. Typing custom free-form descriptions adds a $200 surcharge per class ($550 total), plus $200 for each 1,000 characters beyond the first 1,000 and $100 per class for incomplete applications.


### How long does it take to get a trademark in 2026?


According to the USPTO’s 2026 results, average first-action wait time (from filing to an examiner’s first office action or approval) dropped to 4.1 months, down from 8.2 months in late 2023, and average total disposal time to registration, allowance, or abandonment fell to 9.5 months. Intent-to-use applications and opposed marks take longer, and 37.8% to 45.5% of intent-to-use filings in 2017–2022 cohorts ultimately registered compared with 73.7% to 77% for use-in-commerce filings.


### What are Trademark Class 9 and Class 42 for software and AI?


Most software and AI products file in Trademark Class 9 (downloadable software, mobile apps, and AI hardware) or Trademark Class 42 (software as a service, cloud platforms, and artificial intelligence as a service). In the 12 months ending October 31, 2026, Class 9 led all Nice classes with 88,704 applications, while Class 42 grew 65.5% from its 2023 low to 78,190 applications, with 33.1% of Class 42 filings naming artificial intelligence.


### Does registering a domain name give you trademark rights?


No. Registering a domain name reserves a DNS web address at a registry, not trademark rights in commerce. Another business may already hold a live or pending federal trademark for the same or a confusingly similar name in your Nice class even when` .com` ,` .ai` , or` .app` is open to register, and using an infringing domain in that industry can trigger a trademark dispute or UDRP complaint.

Instant Trademark Search builds its canonical dataset from the USPTO’s complete 2025 annual case-file archive (` TRTYRAP` , 90 parts covering filings through December 31, 2025) merged with all 2026 daily transaction archives (` TRTDXFAP` ) through November 21, 2026, keeping the newest revision of each eight-digit serial number ordered by transaction date, source publication date, object generation, and file name. Status categories (` live` ,` pending` , and` dead` ) map USPTO numeric status codes using the published lifecycle table (` status::categorize` in` trademarks-core` ). Owner nationality reads the first listed owner’s` <nationality>` country or US state of organization (without separate applicant domicile fields). Alphanumeric wordmark comparisons strip punctuation and spaces and convert ASCII letters to one case.
